passage: Baljeet, you ask why your Bua Yamini never shouts? Because I once shouted so loud my own father stopped talking to me for three days. I was sixteen. A friend's cousin was having a sangeet in the next colony, ending at eleven. Papa said no. I said, "Everyone is going! Everyone's parents allow it! You are the strictest father in the world!" I slammed the door so hard the photograph fell. Papa's jaw tightened. "Then everyone's parents can look after everyone," he said. "My answer is no, and it will be no next time also." Mummy tried to soften it, but Papa raised a hand. I sat in my room crying, sure I had been right. Yet I had not asked him one question. I had only given orders.

qa.q: What time was the sangeet due to end?
qa.a: The sangeet was due to end at eleven.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when slamming the door, and what shows it?
qa.a: Yamini was angry, hurt and sure of being right; the shouting and the slammed door show it.

qa.q: What could Yamini have tried instead of shouting, and why?
qa.a: Yamini could have asked what worried Papa and offered a plan such as a ride home, because shouting made Papa dig in while a question would have opened a talk.

qa.q: How did Papa see the shouting?
qa.a: Papa likely saw a challenge to his authority and not a real request, so he held firm and refused even for next time.

grounding: The teen shouts that everyone else is allowed and that parents are too strict, the argument becomes a power struggle, and the request is refused outright.
